title: Collections.checkedList/Map/Set: runtime type enforcement, catching heap pollution
keyPoints: Collections.checkedList(list, type) wraps a collection with runtime type checking that verifies every element on insertion.
Without the checked wrapper, heap pollution causes ClassCastException at retrieval time, far from where the wrong type was inserted.
With the checked wrapper, ClassCastException occurs at insertion time, with a stack trace pointing directly to the buggy code.
checkedMap(map, keyType, valueType) checks both key and value types on every put operation.
The performance overhead is one instanceof check per insertion, which is negligible for most use cases.
Checked wrappers are especially useful when passing collections to legacy code that uses raw types.
The checked wrapper does not prevent heap pollution through the underlying collection reference; always wrap at creation time.

s1_definition.oneliner: Collections.checkedList/Map/Set wraps a collection with runtime type checking on every insertion, catching heap pollution at add time instead of get time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Runtime type enforcement** – every `add()`, `set()`, `put()` call checks `instanceof` against the declared element type; wrong types throw ClassCastException immediately
- **Catches pollution at source** – without the wrapper, a wrong type sneaks in silently and causes ClassCastException later at retrieval; with the wrapper, the exception occurs at insertion with a clear stack trace
- **Three variants** – `checkedList(list, elementType)`, `checkedSet(set, elementType)`, `checkedMap(map, keyType, valueType)`
- **Performance** – one instanceof check per insertion; negligible overhead for most applications
- **Use case** – debugging heap pollution, protecting collections passed to legacy raw-type code, and as a safety net during generics migration
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a normal filing drawer (plain List<String>) accepts anything through the back door (raw type reference). Someone files a number where a name should be. Months later, a clerk reads the drawer and finds the wrong item. The checked wrapper is like a security scanner at the drawer entrance: every item is scanned on filing. If the wrong type is inserted, the scanner rejects it immediately with an alarm that identifies exactly who tried to file the wrong item.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Without Checked Wrapper            With Checked Wrapper
  =======================            =====================

  List<String> list = new ArrayList  List<String> list = checkedList(
  List raw = list                       new ArrayList<>(), String.class)
  raw.add(42) -> silent!             List raw = list
                                     raw.add(42) -> CCE at add!
  list.get(0)                        ┌───────────────────────────┐
  ┌──────────────────────┐           │ Scanner at the entrance:  │
  │ (String) list.get(0) │           │ instanceof String? NO     │
  │ 42 is not String     │           │ -> ClassCastException!    │
  │ -> CCE at GET!       │           │                           │
  │                      │           │ Stack trace points to     │
  │ Stack trace points   │           │ the EXACT add() call      │
  │ to get(), not add()  │           └───────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Collections.checkedList, checkedMap, and checkedSet wrap collections with runtime type checking on every insertion operation. Without the wrapper, heap pollution from raw types causes ClassCastException at retrieval time, with a stack trace pointing to the innocent get() call instead of the buggy add(). With the wrapper, the exception occurs immediately at insertion, with a clear message identifying the wrong type and a stack trace pointing directly to the offending code.

The checked wrapper is not a replacement for generics. Generics catch type errors at compile time, which is always better. Checked collections are a runtime safety net for situations where generics cannot help: legacy code that uses raw types, third-party APIs that bypass type parameters, and debugging sessions where you need to find the source of mysterious ClassCastExceptions.

At National Bank of India, Rajesh wrapped all collections passed to the legacy payment gateway module with Collections.checkedList. When the gateway's raw-type code tried to insert an Integer where a String was expected, the checked wrapper caught it immediately. Without the wrapper, the error would have appeared hours later in the reporting module, three layers removed from the source.

Remember one sentence: Collections.checkedList adds a runtime type scanner on every insertion, catching heap pollution at add time instead of get time, which is essential when integrating with legacy raw-type code.
